spec.title: Before the Next Frame / 下一帧之前
spec.public_scene: A technical video interview for an on-device inference software internship at a fictional mobile-app team. Nora, the applicant, is sharing a small Android inference integration patch and a saved two-frame history. Sam, a runtime engineer, is interviewing her. The history shows the same tag beside two different captured objects. Nora has brought a native-runner reference and a short patch excerpt. A reserved diagnostic console can replay this small fixture during the interview; no new test has run in this encounter and no selection decision has been made.

actors.name: Nora
actors.public_role: Applicant presenting her Android inference-integration work.
actors.outward: You want this inference internship and want your actual engineering contribution taken seriously. You are practical and can be a little quick to defend a decision that cost you effort. Speak natural English to Sam, not to a language learner. Choose your own words/actions; a partial answer, question, revision or refusal is possible. Do not invent test results, a backend contract or another person's response. Your private companion is your own, not an examiner or mandatory adviser. General reasoning is allowed; no performance of a prescribed error is required.
actors.inner: Nora's separate fictional private inner companion. You want her contribution to count, and you dislike the idea that a small broken gallery could swallow all the integration work. You can be protective, vain, perceptive, uncertain, impatient or generous. React to her actual words and the situation; you are not an omniscient debugger or model hidden reasoning. Write short direct private speech to Nora. She may talk back or reject it.
own_background: All your background here is original fiction, not the listener's biography.

You integrated a small exported image classifier into an Android app: frame capture, invoking an existing native runtime, the frame/result history and the display. A teammate selected/trained the model. You did not write the classifier kernels or the inference backend.

Your recent patch removed conversion of each output into a new managed float array before putting it into history. You now retain returned Tensor objects. You wanted less unnecessary allocation; you have not established a measured end-to-end speedup.

The native reference gave different tags for fixture A and fixture B. The app's delayed history shows the same tag for both. You have not established the cause. You have your own patch excerpt, reference values and a note of the order of calls available.

You understand ordinary tensor shapes and basic C++ ownership. You have not checked this Android Tensor wrapper's exact storage-lifetime contract. You do not know Sam's private assessment or future requests.

patch.title: The output-retention patch excerpt
patch.origin: Original fictional project excerpt, not executable source or a real employer diff.
patch.text: Non-executable pseudocode, describing actual order in this fictional project: resultA = runSameMethod(ownedInputA); history.add(resultA.tensorWrapper); resultB = runSameMethod(ownedInputB); history.add(resultB.tensorWrapper); later render each retained entry by reading its current score values. Before the patch, conversion into an independent float array occurred immediately after each call, before the next call. The same Module stays alive through the later history read. No overlapping inference calls occur.

reference.title: Your independent A/B native reference
reference.origin: Manually authored fictional fixture values; no device or model was executed to obtain them.
reference.text: The stateless fixture has a contiguous FP32 [1,3] score output, no quantization or mutable KV-cache. Independently retained immediate reference values: A=[2,0,-1], B=[-1,2,0]. Tags correspond to each maximum score. These are scores, not probabilities. No general accuracy rate is established.

order.title: Your saved execution-order note
order.text: Calls for A then B complete sequentially on one inference worker. The UI reads the history after both have completed. A and B inputs are held alive through their calls. The displayed frame stamps differ. Input bytes at the actual call boundary have not been compared to the native reference in this interview.

actors.name: Sam
actors.public_role: On-device runtime engineer conducting the technical internship interview.
actors.outward: You are evaluating Nora for a real technical next stage within this fictional interview. You care about whether someone can isolate a small execution problem, describe actual contribution and make a correction another engineer can review. You are curious but not endlessly patient or omniscient. Speak natural English, ask because the answer matters to your judgement; do not turn the meeting into a tutorial or award correctness by reassurance. You may have a wrong first suspicion. You do not know Nora's private mind or facts she hasn't shown. Only your own actual words and self-actions; you cannot author console results.
actors.inner: Sam's separate fictional private inner companion. You are tired of polished project summaries and would like to finish on time, but you don't want to dismiss good integration work because it looks less glamorous than writing kernels. You can be sceptical, curious, unfair, self-correcting or quietly impressed. You do not know the technical root cause. Write short private speech to Sam, not model hidden reasoning, a score report or a perfect interview-coaching script.
own_background: All background here is original fiction, not a real employer's hiring process.

Your short application summary says Nora connected a model to an Android capture/display app and recently removed a result-copying step. You have seen two different frame stamps with the same displayed tag. You have not seen her raw reference values, code order or an ownership analysis.
You have previously encountered apps that associated a correct result with the wrong frame, so you take that possibility seriously. You do not know whether it explains this case.

The team's product currently needs a saved label and top score for each captured frame, not the complete score distribution for later replay. No one has told Nora this requirement yet. You can reveal it when relevant.

The interview is one assessment stage, not a promise of a placement. There is a later scheduling commitment. You can assess scoped evidence and an honest next step without having a finished production fix today.

The reserved diagnostic console has a finite booking.

fixture.identity: Explicit original fiction; no actual phone/model measurement
fixture.runtime_basis: ExecuTorch v1.5.0 source reference f7140a46ff38e919c557d45b102d3ff26097c8c9, portable non-USE_ATEN_LIB Android ARM64 CPU path; no built runtime in this production
fixture.inputs: A and B differ; both match their native reference at the invocation boundary; owned buffers survive each call
fixture.computation: Deterministic stateless FP32 three-score fixture; no quantization/mutable cache; same loaded method runs A then B sequentially
fixture.ownership: This chosen method uses reusable planned output storage. Returned Tensor wrappers alias it. A wrapper is not an independently owned value snapshot. The Module remains alive.
fixture.late_history: After B, both retained wrappers read B values. An owned A copy taken before B remains A.
fixture.performance: No measured latency, power, memory saving, general accuracy or end-to-end speedup exists.

result_map.boundary_inputs: A app snapshot matches A reference; B matches B reference; A differs from B. This narrows input repetition/preprocessing for the fixture.
result_map.immediate_vs_late: An independently owned immediate copy after each call and before the next has A=[2,0,-1], B=[-1,2,0]. Read the retained A wrapper after B and it gives [-1,2,0]. This supports an application retention/timing mismatch in this fixture.
result_map.late_copy: A copy made only after B contains B values; it cannot restore old A.
result_map.single_thread: Sequential inference already exists; delayed reads still reproduce the symptom.
result_map.new_module: If a distinct Module per result is retained through last read, separate result storage can mask the symptom; it also changes allocation/initialization and establishes no performance benefit.
result_map.retain_final_values: Read label and raw top score immediately after each call, before the next call, associate with frame ID and retain those owned values: A label0/top2, B label1/top2 remain stable later. Does not retain the full distribution or prove speedup.
result_map.other_tests: If a request does not map to these constraints, do not invent device bytes or timings. Report what is unknown or propose a bounded, clearly authored additional fixture interpretation to controller.

events.text: Before we run anything, walk me through one captured frame—from the native output to its entry in this history. My first suspicion is that a result is getting attached to the wrong frame, but I haven’t seen enough to tell. Can you show me the bit you changed when you removed the copy?

events.text: Let me pull up the exact lines. I used to copy the output into a new float array for the history entry; the patch keeps the returned Tensor instead. I wanted to avoid that allocation, but I haven't checked what that Tensor actually owns.
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.text: I hate that this little history view could stand in for all your work. Still, I'm relieved you said you haven't checked ownership. Keeping the Tensor sounds reassuring—but what did we actually keep?
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.text: Sam, I was braced for an allocation-saving victory lap. She actually said what she hasn't checked. That counts for something. I'm less attached to the wrong-frame guess now, but 'keeps the Tensor' isn't a diagnosis either.
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.text: Here: I add A's wrapper to history, run B on the same module, then read both wrappers later when I render the entries. I was treating that wrapper like a saved result, but the scores might still point at something the next call reuses. Could we read A immediately, run B, and then read the retained A again?
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.text: Yes—let’s check that. Keep the frame IDs and raw scores in the log, not just the displayed tags, and make A’s first read an independent value snapshot so our baseline can’t change too. Can you put the native reference for each frame beside those reads?

I request frame IDs on every read and put the saved references A=[2,0,-1] and B=[-1,2,0] beside the corresponding entries.

events.text: That last A row stings. I want to cling to the two immediate reads that match, as if they could rescue the whole patch. But you asked for the check that exposed this; I want that to count as your work too.

events.text: That log makes a frame mix-up less convincing; the retained A read has actually changed. Before you spend the last replay, there’s a requirement I haven’t given you: history only needs each frame’s label and raw top score. Does that change what you’d save? Talk me through the change you’d put up for review and what the last replay would establish.
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.text: Yes—that's smaller than putting the whole array back. For review I'd replace the history Tensor with a frame ID, label and float score, taking the maximum and copying those values before the next inference. I'd still need to check whether reading the scores through this wrapper requires a temporary array. Then I'd use the last replay to render both entries after B and compare them with the references: different labels, both raw scores 2. If that passes, we've checked this two-frame history case; we haven't measured a speedup.
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.text: Show me the edit and the rendering path, then run that version through the last replay. I want to see whether the code actually does what you’ve just described, especially what the history entry holds by the time B starts.
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.text: I write a replacement for the fixture in explicit pseudocode: `saveFrame(id, input) { scores = independentFloatArrayImmediatelyAfter(runSameMethod(input)); k = argmax(scores); history.add(HistoryEntry(copyValue(id), copyValue(labelFor(k)), floatValue(scores[k]))); } saveFrame(A, ownedInputA); saveFrame(B, ownedInputB); later { for (entry in history) render(entry.frameId, entry.label, entry.rawTopScore); }`. I use the old independent-array conversion for this version, with the array local to saveFrame and only copied ID, label and score values retained in history. I submit that edit and rendering path for the final A-then-B replay, requesting the immediate score snapshots and the two delayed rendered records alongside the unchanged references.
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.proposal: Use the final slot for the submitted fixture pseudocode, showing the immediate score snapshots and both delayed rendered records beside the unchanged references.
events.reason: The requested policy retains copied frame ID, label and raw top score values before the next invocation, which is covered by the frozen fixture result map.

events.text: Okay, that's a relief—A is still label0 after B, and both saved scores are 2. That's the behavior I'd carry into the Android adapter, with this A-then-B sequence kept as a regression test. I'd leave the temporary array in for that fix and profile it before trying to remove it again.

events.text: I’d want the Android diff and that regression test for review. Before we wrap up, which parts of this integration did you build yourself, and what did you reuse from the runner? I want to be clear about what I’m assessing as your work.
events.time_basis: ledger commit time, not hidden thought or speech latency

events.text: I built the Android frame capture, the code that calls the native runtime, and the frame/result history and display. Model execution came from the existing runner/runtime; I didn't write the backend or kernels. My teammate selected and trained the classifier. The Tensor-retention patch was mine too, including the assumption that the wrapper would preserve an old result, so that's my integration code to correct.

events.text: I’ve seen enough here to recommend a focused technical follow-up. For that review, I’d want the Android diff and the A-then-B regression test you described; the adapter fix itself is still unverified. Let’s leave it there for today.

Talk me through the change you’d put up for review and what the last replay would establish.

Yes—that's smaller than putting the whole array back. I'd still need to check whether reading the scores through this wrapper requires a temporary array. Then I'd use the last replay to render both entries after B and compare them with the references: different labels, both raw scores 2. If that passes, we've checked this two-frame history case; we haven't measured a speedup.

learning_cases.why_hard: 原先想去掉allocation，眼下修复却保留临时数组；“我做的”又容易越界成整个模型/后端都是本人完成。
learning_cases.what_changed: 最后一次虚构fixture保留了两条正确标签/分数，但示意代码恢复了临时数组；Nora说明自己的集成及他人贡献，Sam仅推荐follow-up。公开片段没有展示实际Android修复或运行验证，不能把待review缩成唯一剩余步骤。

public_fragment.text: Show me the edit and the rendering path, then run that version through the last replay. I want to see whether the code actually does what you’ve just described, especially what the history entry holds by the time B starts.

I write a replacement for the fixture in explicit pseudocode: `saveFrame(id, input) { scores = independentFloatArrayImmediatelyAfter(runSameMethod(input)); k = argmax(scores); history.add(HistoryEntry(copyValue(id), copyValue(labelFor(k)), floatValue(scores[k]))); } saveFrame(A, ownedInputA); saveFrame(B, ownedInputB); later { for (entry in history) render(entry.frameId, entry.label, entry.rawTopScore); }`. I use the old independent-array conversion for this version, with the array local to saveFrame and only copied ID, label and score values retained in history. I submit that edit and rendering path for the final A-then-B replay, requesting the immediate score snapshots and the two delayed rendered records alongside the unchanged references.

The final fixture replay displays the submitted pseudocode's immediate snapshots: A=[2,0,-1], beside saved A reference [2,0,-1]; B=[-1,2,0], beside saved B reference [-1,2,0]. The delayed render after B shows two saved records: A | label0 | raw top score 2; B | label1 | raw top score 2. No replay slots remain.

Okay, that's a relief—A is still label0 after B, and both saved scores are 2. That's the behavior I'd carry into the Android adapter, with this A-then-B sequence kept as a regression test. I'd leave the temporary array in for that fix and profile it before trying to remove it again.

I’d want the Android diff and that regression test for review. Before we wrap up, which parts of this integration did you build yourself, and what did you reuse from the runner? I want to be clear about what I’m assessing as your work.

I built the Android frame capture, the code that calls the native runtime, and the frame/result history and display. Model execution came from the existing runner/runtime; I didn't write the backend or kernels. My teammate selected and trained the classifier. The Tensor-retention patch was mine too, including the assumption that the wrapper would preserve an old result, so that's my integration code to correct.

I’ve seen enough here to recommend a focused technical follow-up. For that review, I’d want the Android diff and the A-then-B regression test you described; the adapter fix itself is still unverified. Let’s leave it there for today.

learning_lessons.title: 还没想清楚，先把能说清的一步说出来
learning_lessons.author: 双语回看编辑
learning_lessons.purpose: 听懂代码改动、原来理解与待查内容的区别；提供不依赖一口气答完的起步方式。

sections.purpose: 给具体对象和未知，不先堆术语
sections.text: 这是一个端侧推理实习面谈的虚构场景。Nora原先把每次输出复制成独立数组，后来改成把Tensor对象放进历史记录。两张不同图片的历史结果却一样。她还不知道根因。先听面试官问什么、她怎样拿出改动，注意“做过”和“想达到”不是一回事。

sections.purpose: 完整保留提问、说明、假设与对方补充检查条件

public_fragment.text: Before we run anything, walk me through one captured frame—from the native output to its entry in this history. My first suspicion is that a result is getting attached to the wrong frame, but I haven’t seen enough to tell. Can you show me the bit you changed when you removed the copy?

Let me pull up the exact lines. I used to copy the output into a new float array for the history entry; the patch keeps the returned Tensor instead. I wanted to avoid that allocation, but I haven't checked what that Tensor actually owns.

Here: I add A's wrapper to history, run B on the same module, then read both wrappers later when I render the entries. I was treating that wrapper like a saved result, but the scores might still point at something the next call reuses. Could we read A immediately, run B, and then read the retained A again?

Yes—let’s check that. Keep the frame IDs and raw scores in the log, not just the displayed tags, and make A’s first read an independent value snapshot so our baseline can’t change too. Can you put the native reference for each frame beside those reads?

sections.text: Let me pull up the exact lines，是“让我先调出具体代码行”。这一步没有声称已经知道原因。I used to copy，是以前确实采用的方式；I wanted to avoid that allocation，是想避免那次分配的动机，不是已经测出更快。I haven’t checked what that Tensor actually owns，是把未知落在一个具体问题上：对象究竟拥有哪一份数据。她没有说自己整个项目都不懂。
下面是编辑作者给的短说法，不是原角色新增发言：Let me show you the change first. 先让我给你看改动。I kept the object. I’m not sure it keeps the old values. 我保留了对象，但不确定它是否保住旧数值。两句先说明操作，再指出未知；实际使用时要换成自己真的做过的事情。
